title: Sensex Diwali Rally Faces Test Beyond Festive Sentiment, Analysts Say
excerpt: A Mint analysis of Bloomberg data shows the Sensex's 8.78% pre-Muhurat surge was the biggest in three decades, but in 6 of 19 comparable years the gains did not last — and analysts say foreign cash buying, crude and Q2 earnings will decide this one.
body:
• The Sensex rose 8.78% in the week before Muhurat trading on November 8 — the biggest pre-Diwali weekly gain in a Mint analysis of Bloomberg data from 1997 to 2026 — and added 0.73% in the week after.
  • History is mixed, not a promise: the Sensex extended a positive pre-Muhurat week in 13 of 19 such years, fell in six, and some reversals were sharp, including a 4.04% fall after a 4.86% gain in 2010.
  • Analysts cited by Mint say the rally holds only if foreign buying continues in cash equities, crude stays contained and second-quarter earnings justify valuations.
  • For diaspora investors in Indian equities, the practical read is to judge the next few weeks on flows and earnings, not on the festive pattern alone — the index already slipped 318.56 points on November 13 while still ending that week higher.

The question hanging over Dalal Street is a data question, not a sentiment one. The BSE Sensex gained 0.73% in the week after Muhurat trading on November 8, adding to an 8.78% surge in the week before it, according to a Mint analysis of Bloomberg data from 1997 to 2026 published via TradingView. That pre-Muhurat surge was the biggest in the three-decade sample, well above the previous high of 5.4% in 2002.

An advance that far outside the historical range cuts both ways: it confirms strong buying, but no earlier year in the sample started from a move this large, so the seasonal pattern has less to say about what follows.

What 30 years of Diwali weeks actually show

Mint found the Sensex rose in the week after Muhurat in 19 of the 29 years through 2025, almost two-thirds of the time. It gained in the week before Muhurat in 19 of 30 years, with advances ranging from 0.03% in 2006 to this year's 8.78%.

A positive lead-up did not guarantee another week of gains: of 19 such years, the Sensex extended gains in 13, including this year, and fell in six. Reversals could be sharp — in 2010 a 4.86% gain was followed by a 4.04% loss, and in 2013 a 2.69% advance by a 2.50% fall.

Buying sometimes continued — in 2001 a 3.29% pre-Muhurat rise was followed by another 5.42%, and in 2025 a 1.02% gain by 2.20%. The averages need caution: across 30 years the average post-Muhurat gain was 1.53%, but that includes a 24.93% surge in 2008 after an 11.89% fall the week before. Excluding 2008, the average drops to 0.72%; the median was 1.01%. In seven of the 11 years with a negative pre-Muhurat week, the index rebounded the following week.

What analysts say has to happen next

Rajesh Singla, CEO and fund manager at Alpha AMC, attributed the pre-Muhurat surge, as reported by Mint, to renewed foreign buying, falling crude prices and short covering — a driver that can lift an index quickly without amounting to fresh long-term buying.

"For it to last, foreign buying must continue in cash equities, crude must stay contained, and Q2 earnings must justify current valuations."

— Rajesh Singla, CEO and fund manager, Alpha AMC, via Mint

Singla urged caution about conclusions from just 30 observations, Mint reported, and would watch whether foreign investors move from covering shorts in index futures to steady cash-market purchases, alongside crude and the rupee. Puneet Singhania of Master Capital Services said festive optimism should not be treated as a reliable seasonal trend, and that consistent inflows, improving earnings and wider participation would indicate greater confidence.

The first test arrived on November 13

The fragility analysts described was visible within days. On November 13 the Sensex fell 318.56 points, or 0.39%, to close at 81,592.45, and the Nifty fell 155.05 points, or 0.61%, to 25,144.30, snapping a three-session winning streak, according to Moneycontrol's market report published via TradingView. Moneycontrol put the week's gain at 0.7% for the Sensex and 0.45% for the Nifty, and cited retail inflation of 6.09% in October, above the Reserve Bank of India's 6% upper tolerance limit.

That combination — a weekly gain preserved, a daily fall on inflation and broad selling — is why the pattern alone does not settle the question. Gains lasted in 13 of 19 comparable years and failed in six, and this year's 8.78% starting point is the largest in the sample, which makes the historical guide weaker, not stronger.

What to watch

On the analysts' own terms, watch whether foreign buying continues in cash equities, whether crude stays contained, whether the rupee steadies, and whether second-quarter earnings justify valuations. Singla's summary, reported by Mint, was blunt: "A few weeks of flows and earnings will tell us more than one strong week." That, not the festival calendar, is the test this rally now has to pass.
